sciATM: Which layer is the coldest, reaching about −90 °C at its top?
The mesosphere is the coldest layer because it has little ozone to absorb sunlight and is far from the warm ground.
In the troposphere, what usually happens to the temperature as you go higher?
The troposphere is heated from the ground up, so the air gets colder with height.
Why does the temperature rise with height in the stratosphere?
Ozone absorbs ultraviolet light from the Sun
Clouds trap heat from the ground there
Nitrogen there burns and releases heat
Jet engines release heat in that layer
Ozone in the stratosphere absorbs the Sun's UV rays and warms the upper part of the layer.
What happens to air pressure as you climb higher in the atmosphere?
Higher up there is less air above you pressing down, so air pressure drops.
Which layer holds about three-quarters of the mass of the atmosphere?
Gravity pulls most air close to the ground, so the thin troposphere holds about 75% of the atmosphere's mass.
What is the boundary between the troposphere and the stratosphere called?
The tropopause marks the top of the troposphere, where the stratosphere begins.
Which gas makes up a little under 1% of Earth's atmosphere?
Argon is the third most common gas in dry air, at about 0.9%.
Which gas makes up only about 0.04% of the air but helps trap heat near Earth?
Carbon dioxide is a greenhouse gas that traps heat even though it is a tiny part of the air.
In which layer can temperatures pass 1000 °C, even though the air is too thin to feel hot?
The thermosphere absorbs intense solar radiation, so its few particles are very hot.
Which list orders the layers from Earth's surface upward?
Going up from the ground, the layers are the troposphere, stratosphere, mesosphere, thermosphere and then the exosphere.
In which layer do almost all clouds and rain form?
Nearly all water vapour is in the troposphere, so clouds and precipitation form there.
Which layer reaches the farthest, up to about 10 000 km above Earth?
The exosphere is the very thin outermost layer that slowly fades into space.
Why is it harder to breathe on top of a very high mountain?
The air is thinner, so each breath has less oxygen
The air there is mostly carbon dioxide instead
Oxygen sinks down into the rocks below
The ozone layer blocks oxygen at that height
Air pressure is lower up high, so each breath holds fewer oxygen molecules.
On average, about how high does the troposphere reach?
The troposphere extends roughly 8 to 15 km up, about 12 km on average.
The ozone layer protects living things by absorbing most of the Sun's …
Ozone absorbs most harmful UV radiation before it reaches the ground.
Which layer lies directly above the stratosphere?
Going upward, the mesosphere comes right after the stratosphere.
Which layer lies directly below the exosphere?
The thermosphere is the layer just beneath the outermost exosphere.
Which layer lies directly above the troposphere?
The stratosphere starts at the tropopause, right above the troposphere.
Weather balloons often rise to about 30 km before they burst. Which layer is that?
The stratosphere runs from about 12 km to 50 km, so 30 km is inside it.
About what percent of Earth's atmosphere is nitrogen?
Nitrogen is the most common gas in the air, at about 78%.
What keeps the atmosphere held around Earth instead of drifting into space?
Earth's gravity pulls on the gas particles and holds the atmosphere in place.
Long-distance passenger jets often cruise just above the weather, in the lowest part of which layer?
Jets can fly in the lower stratosphere, above most of the clouds and storms of the troposphere.
sciNWT: Which of Newton's laws explains this? A swimmer pushes water backward and glides forward.
The swimmer pushes on the water and the water pushes back on the swimmer with an equal and opposite force.
Which of Newton's laws explains this? A soccer ball kicked harder speeds up more.
A larger net force on the same mass gives a larger acceleration, as F = ma says.
Which of Newton's laws explains this? A tablecloth yanked quickly from under dishes leaves the dishes in place.
The dishes have inertia and tend to stay at rest when the cloth is pulled away quickly.
Which of Newton's laws explains this? Seatbelts stop riders from flying forward when a car stops suddenly.
Riders keep moving forward because of inertia unless a force, like a seatbelt, stops them.
Which of Newton's laws explains this? A balloon zooms forward as air rushes out of its back.
The balloon pushes air backward and the air pushes the balloon forward.
Which of Newton's laws explains this? A truck needs a much larger engine force than a car to reach the same acceleration.
A larger mass needs a larger force for the same acceleration, as F = ma says.
Which of Newton's laws explains this? A hockey puck slides a long way across smooth ice.
With very little friction, the puck keeps moving at nearly the same speed because of inertia.
Which of Newton's laws explains this? When you jump, you push down on the ground and the ground pushes you up.
Your push on the ground is matched by an equal and opposite push from the ground on you.
Which of Newton's laws explains this? A coin on a card over a cup drops into the cup when the card is flicked away.
The coin's inertia keeps it in place while the card moves, so gravity then pulls it into the cup.
Which of Newton's laws explains this? Paddling backward on the water moves a canoe forward.
The paddle pushes water backward and the water pushes the canoe forward.
Which of Newton's laws explains this? An astronaut in space throws a tool forward and drifts backward.
The astronaut pushes the tool forward and the tool pushes the astronaut backward with an equal force.
A net force of 20 N acts on a 4 kg box. What is its acceleration?
Using a = F ÷ m, 20 N ÷ 4 kg = 5 m/s².
What net force is needed to accelerate a 1000 kg car at 2 m/s²?
Using F = ma, 1000 kg × 2 m/s² = 2000 N.
A 0.5 kg ball accelerates at 10 m/s². What net force acts on it?
Using F = ma, 0.5 kg × 10 m/s² = 5 N.
A net force of 30 N gives an object an acceleration of 6 m/s². What is its mass?
Using m = F ÷ a, 30 N ÷ 6 m/s² = 5 kg.
An object's resistance to changes in its motion
The force that pulls objects toward Earth
The speed at which an object is travelling
The rubbing force between two surfaces
Inertia is the tendency of an object to keep doing what it is already doing.
Which object has the most inertia?
Inertia depends on mass, and the loaded truck has by far the most mass.
How do the two forces in an action–reaction pair compare?
Equal in size and opposite in direction
Equal in size and in the same direction
Unequal, with the action force larger
Unequal, with the reaction force larger
Newton's third law says the forces in a pair are always equal and opposite.
Why don't action–reaction forces cancel each other out?
They act on the same object
They are not equal in size
They point in the same direction
Forces only cancel when they act on the same object, and each force in a pair acts on a different object.
The net force on a moving object becomes zero. What does the object do?
Keeps moving at a constant velocity
Speeds up at a steady rate
By the first law, with no net force an object keeps its speed and direction.
The same force is applied to an object with twice the mass. What happens to its acceleration?
Since a = F ÷ m, doubling the mass halves the acceleration.
What is the SI unit of force, equal to 1 kg·m/s²?
One newton is the force that gives 1 kg an acceleration of 1 m/s².
sciXsTransW: A wave has a frequency of 4 Hz and a wavelength of 3 m. What is its speed?
Wave speed = frequency × wavelength = 4 Hz × 3 m = 12 m/s.
A wave travels at 20 m/s with a wavelength of 4 m. What is its frequency?
A wave travels at 30 m/s with a frequency of 10 Hz. What is its wavelength?
What is the SI unit of frequency?
Frequency is measured in hertz (Hz), meaning waves per second.
In which unit is wavelength measured?
Wavelength is a distance, so it is measured in metres.
A wave has a period of 0.5 s. What is its frequency?
Which of these is NOT a transverse wave?
A wave on a skipping rope
Sound in air is a longitudinal wave, where particles vibrate back and forth along the wave's direction.
Which of these is a transverse wave?
Microwaves are electromagnetic waves, which are transverse.
You shake a rope with bigger up-and-down motions. What happens to the energy the wave carries?
A larger amplitude means the wave carries more energy.
The middle line that a transverse wave moves above and below is the…
The rest position is where the medium sits when there is no wave.
A crest rises 0.4 m above the rest position. What is the amplitude?
Amplitude is measured from the rest position to a crest, so it is 0.4 m.
The vertical distance from a crest down to a trough is 1 m. What is the amplitude?
Amplitude is half the crest-to-trough height, so 1 m ÷ 2 = 0.5 m.
Exactly four complete waves fit along 8 m of rope. What is the wavelength?
Ten waves pass a point in 2 s. What is the frequency?
What does a transverse wave carry from one place to another?
Waves move energy, while the medium only moves up and down around its rest position.
Two waves travel along the same rope at the same speed. Wave A has the higher frequency. Wave A has the…
At the same speed, a higher frequency means the waves are packed closer together.
S (secondary) waves shake the ground side to side, perpendicular to their direction of travel.
Through which can S waves, the transverse earthquake waves, travel?
S waves need a rigid medium, so they cannot pass through liquids like Earth's outer core.
A crest and the next trough are 1.5 m apart, measured along the wave. What is the wavelength?
A crest to the next trough is half a wavelength, so the wavelength is 2 × 1.5 m = 3 m.
What is the period of a wave?
The time for one complete wave to pass
The height of a crest above rest
The number of crests in a metre
The period is the time for one full wave cycle, measured in seconds.
A water wave moves at 2 m/s with a frequency of 0.5 Hz. What is its wavelength?
Shaking a rope more times each second increases the wave's…
More waves made per second means a higher frequency.
sciWaveP: Wave A has a wavelength of 2 m and wave B has a wavelength of 5 m. Both travel at the same speed. Which has the higher frequency?
At equal speeds, the wave with the shorter wavelength has the higher frequency.
Two sounds travel through air: one at 200 Hz and one at 800 Hz. Which has the longer wavelength?
At the same speed, the lower frequency sound has the longer wavelength.
A wave's amplitude doubles but nothing else changes. What happens to its frequency?
Amplitude and frequency are separate properties, so changing one does not change the other.
Which colour of visible light has the longest wavelength?
Red light has the longest wavelength in the visible spectrum, about 700 nm.
Which colour of visible light has the highest frequency?
Violet light has the shortest wavelength and therefore the highest frequency of visible light.
A sound wave travels at 340 m/s with a frequency of 170 Hz. What is its wavelength?
A whisper and a shout are at the same pitch. Which property mainly differs?
Loudness depends on amplitude, so the shout has a larger amplitude.
A dog whistle is too high-pitched for people to hear. Compared with everyday sounds, its waves have a…
Pitch depends on frequency, and sounds too high for humans have very high frequencies.
The frequency of a wave is halved while its speed stays the same. What happens to its wavelength?
Since wavelength = speed ÷ frequency, halving the frequency doubles the wavelength.
Which ocean wave carries more energy?
The taller wave has the larger amplitude, so it carries more energy.
Wave A has crests 4 cm apart. Wave B has crests 8 cm apart. Which has the longer wavelength?
Wavelength is the crest-to-crest distance, and 8 cm is longer than 4 cm.
Wave A's crests rise 3 cm above rest. Wave B's crests rise 6 cm above rest. How do their amplitudes compare?
B's amplitude is four times A's
Amplitude is the height above rest, and 6 cm is twice 3 cm.
For electromagnetic waves, a higher frequency means…
Higher-frequency electromagnetic waves, like X-rays, carry more energy than low-frequency ones like radio.
A 10 Hz wave and a 20 Hz wave travel on the same string at the same speed. How does the 20 Hz wave's wavelength compare?
Doubling the frequency at the same speed halves the wavelength.
A guitarist plucks the same string harder. What changes about the sound wave?
Plucking harder makes bigger vibrations, increasing amplitude and loudness, not pitch.
Pressing a guitar string against a fret makes the note higher. What has increased?
A shorter vibrating string vibrates faster, raising the frequency and pitch.
Which has the shorter wavelength: radio waves or X-rays?
X-rays have wavelengths far shorter than radio waves, which can be metres long.
A wave has a period of 0.1 s. What is its frequency?
Wave A has a frequency of 5 Hz and wave B has 15 Hz. Which has the shorter period?
Period = 1 ÷ frequency, so the higher-frequency wave has the shorter period.
A wave enters a medium where it travels twice as fast, but its frequency stays the same. Its wavelength…
Since wavelength = speed ÷ frequency, doubling the speed doubles the wavelength.
Which wave has the greatest amplitude?
One with crests 5 cm above rest
One with crests 2 cm above rest
One with crests 1 cm above rest
One with crests 3 cm above rest
Amplitude is the height of the crest above rest, and 5 cm is the greatest.
Which three quantities are linked by the equation v = fλ?
In v = fλ, v is wave speed, f is frequency and λ is wavelength.
sciXsTRA: What is happening to the wave? Sunlight warming a dark asphalt road
The dark road takes in the light's energy, which turns into heat.
What is happening to the wave? Light passing through clear water in a glass
Clear water lets light pass through it, so the light is transmitted.
What is happening to the wave? A bat's call bouncing off a moth and back to the bat
The sound bounces off the moth and returns as an echo, so it is reflected.
What is happening to the wave? Sunlight bouncing off the Moon toward Earth
The Moon makes no light of its own; it reflects sunlight back to us.
What is happening to the wave? X-rays passing through skin and muscle
Soft tissue lets most X-rays pass through it to the film or detector.
What is happening to the wave? X-rays stopped by bones, so bones look white on the image
Dense bone absorbs X-rays, so fewer reach the detector behind it.
What is happening to the wave? Ultrasound bouncing off an unborn baby to make an image
Ultrasound echoes reflect off tissues, and the machine turns the echoes into an image.
What is happening to the wave? Microwaves taken in by soup, heating it up
Water in the soup absorbs microwave energy and warms up.
What is happening to the wave? Music from next door passing through the wall
The sound travels through the wall material, so it is transmitted.
What is happening to the wave? Foam panels in a recording studio soaking up sound
Soft foam absorbs sound energy so it does not echo around the room.
What is happening to the wave? A sonar pulse bouncing off the sea floor back to a ship
The sound pulse bounces back from the sea floor, so it is reflected.
What is happening to the wave? Sunlight passing through a car's windshield
Clear glass lets visible light pass through, so the light is transmitted.
What is happening to the wave? Radar waves bouncing off an aeroplane back to the radar dish
Radar works by detecting waves reflected from objects like planes.
What is happening to the wave? Earthquake waves passing through rock to a distant seismograph
The seismic waves travel through the rock, so they are transmitted.
Which material would best absorb sound in a noisy room?
Soft, thick materials like carpet absorb sound instead of reflecting it.
A smooth, shiny mirror reflects almost all the light that hits it.
Clear glass lets light pass through, while the others block it.
Why does a white shirt stay cooler in the sun than a black shirt?
It reflects more of the light
It absorbs more of the light
White reflects most light, so less energy is absorbed and turned into heat.
Why does a red apple look red?
It reflects red light and absorbs the rest
It absorbs red light and reflects the rest
It transmits every colour except red
It gives off its own red light
We see the colour of light an object reflects into our eyes.
When a wave is absorbed, what happens to its energy?
It changes into another form, often heat
It is sent back the way it came
Energy cannot be destroyed, so absorbed wave energy usually becomes thermal energy.
A material that lets no light pass through is called…
Opaque materials reflect or absorb all light, so none is transmitted.
Frosted glass lets some light through but blurs what is behind it. It is…
Translucent materials transmit some light but scatter it so images are not clear.
sciEMwave: Which electromagnetic waves have the shortest wavelength?
Gamma rays are at the high-energy end of the spectrum, with the shortest wavelengths.
Which electromagnetic waves carry AM and FM broadcasts?
Radio stations send their signals using radio waves.
Which waves are used in radiation therapy to destroy cancer cells?
High-energy gamma rays can be aimed to damage and kill cancer cells.
Which list goes from longest to shortest wavelength?
Wavelength shrinks from radio through infrared and ultraviolet to gamma rays.
Which colour of visible light has the lowest energy?
Red light has the lowest frequency of visible light, so it carries the least energy.
Do electromagnetic waves need a medium to travel through?
No, they can travel through a vacuum
Yes, they need air to travel
Yes, they need water to travel
Yes, they need a solid to travel
Electromagnetic waves are vibrating fields, so they can cross empty space, like sunlight reaching Earth.
About how fast does light travel in a vacuum?
Light and all electromagnetic waves travel at about 300 000 km per second in a vacuum.
What kind of waves are electromagnetic waves?
The electric and magnetic fields vibrate at right angles to the direction the wave travels.
Black lights give off which invisible waves that make some posters glow?
Black lights give off UV, which fluorescent paints absorb and re-emit as visible light.
Which part of the spectrum lies between infrared and ultraviolet?
Visible light sits between infrared (longer) and ultraviolet (shorter) wavelengths.
Which part of the spectrum lies between radio waves and infrared?
Microwaves have wavelengths shorter than radio waves but longer than infrared.
Which part of the spectrum lies between ultraviolet and gamma rays?
X-rays have shorter wavelengths than ultraviolet but longer than gamma rays.
Moving across the spectrum, as wavelength gets shorter, frequency…
All electromagnetic waves travel at the same speed, so shorter wavelengths mean higher frequencies.
Which waves does the ozone layer mostly absorb?
The ozone layer absorbs most of the Sun's harmful ultraviolet radiation.
Why are X-rays and gamma rays dangerous in large doses?
They carry enough energy to damage cells and DNA
They are loud enough to harm the ears
They make the body much too cold
They have very long, heavy wavelengths
These high-energy waves can break chemical bonds in DNA and harm living cells.
Large dish telescopes that detect signals from distant gas clouds use which waves?
Radio telescopes collect long-wavelength radio waves given off by objects in space.
Which waves let thermal cameras see warm bodies in the dark?
Warm objects give off infrared, which thermal cameras detect.
White light passes through a prism. What comes out the other side?
A prism bends each colour by a different amount, splitting white light into a spectrum.
Which electromagnetic waves have the lowest frequency?
Radio waves have the longest wavelengths and therefore the lowest frequencies.
Which waves do airport security scanners use to see inside bags?
X-rays pass through soft materials but are blocked by dense objects, showing what is inside.
What are electromagnetic waves made of?
Electromagnetic waves are linked electric and magnetic fields that vibrate together.
A station broadcasts at 100 MHz. Which part of the spectrum is this?
FM radio stations broadcast around 88 to 108 MHz, in the radio part of the spectrum.
sciXsInfra: A security light switches on when someone walks past at night. What does its sensor detect?
Infrared given off by the person's body
Ultraviolet given off by the person's skin
X-rays given off by the person's bones
Gamma rays given off by the person's cells
Motion sensors detect the infrared radiation that warm bodies give off.
How does a toaster brown bread?
Its hot coils give off infrared that heats the bread
Its hot coils give off X-rays that cook the bread
Its coils give off sound that shakes the bread
Its coils give off gamma rays that dry the bread
Glowing hot coils radiate infrared energy, which the bread absorbs as heat.
Infrared lies just beyond which colour of visible light?
Red
Violet
Blue
Green
The name infrared means 'below red', since its wavelengths are just longer than red light.
Compared with visible light, infrared has a…
longer wavelength
shorter wavelength
higher frequency
faster speed
Infrared waves are longer than visible light waves and have lower frequencies.
Weather satellites use infrared images to…
see clouds at night by their temperature
measure the thickness of the ozone
listen to thunder from space
see through the ground
Infrared shows temperature differences, so clouds can be tracked even without sunlight.
Who discovered infrared in 1800 by placing a thermometer just past the red end of a spectrum?
William Herschel
Isaac Newton
Marie Curie
Albert Einstein
Herschel noticed the thermometer warmed beyond red light, revealing invisible infrared.
Why are thermal images useful for checking a house in winter?
They show where heat escapes from the house
They show the colour of the paint
They show sound leaking from rooms
They show where X-rays enter
Warm spots on a thermal image reveal leaks around windows, doors and walls.
Why do search-and-rescue teams use infrared cameras?
To find warm people in the dark
To hear calls for help from afar
To see through solid rock
To measure the depth of lakes
People are warmer than their surroundings, so they show up clearly on infrared cameras.
Fibre-optic internet cables usually carry signals as pulses of…
infrared light
ultraviolet light
X-rays
gamma rays
Most fibre-optic systems use invisible infrared light because it travels far through glass fibres.
How does a TV remote control send its signal?
Flashes of infrared light
Pulses of X-rays
Flashes of ultraviolet
Bursts of gamma rays
The remote flashes an infrared LED in a code that a sensor on the TV reads.
Why might a TV remote stop working when your hand covers its front end?
Your hand blocks the infrared beam
Your hand cools down the batteries
Your hand reflects radio waves away
Your hand adds static to the TV
Infrared from the remote needs a clear path to the TV's sensor, and your hand absorbs it.
Which of these gives off the most infrared radiation?
A hot stove element
An ice cube
A cold drink can
A snowball
Hotter objects give off much more infrared than cold ones.
Why do some space telescopes observe in infrared?
Infrared passes through dust that blocks visible light
Infrared is the only light that stars give off
Infrared travels faster than visible light
Infrared makes far-off stars look closer
Infrared can pass through clouds of cosmic dust, revealing stars and galaxies hidden in visible light.
Physiotherapists sometimes use infrared lamps to…
warm and relax sore muscles
take pictures of bones
help skin make vitamin D
kill germs on the skin
Infrared lamps gently heat tissue, which can ease muscle pain.
Farmers use infrared images taken by drones to…
spot crops that are stressed or unhealthy
hear insects chewing on the leaves
see minerals deep underground
count raindrops falling in a storm
Healthy and stressed plants reflect and give off infrared differently, which shows up in the images.
An ear thermometer measures temperature by detecting…
infrared from the eardrum
ultraviolet from the eardrum
sound from the ear canal
X-rays from the skull
The warm eardrum gives off infrared, and the thermometer turns that reading into a temperature.
Why do you feel warm facing a campfire, even on a cool night?
Infrared from the fire reaches your skin
Ultraviolet from the fire heats your bones
Smoke carries the heat by conduction
Sound from the crackling warms you
The fire radiates infrared, which travels through the air and is absorbed by your skin.
Infrared heat lamps are used on farms to…
keep newborn chicks warm
keep chicks cool in summer
make hens lay blue eggs
scare foxes away at night
Young chicks cannot keep themselves warm, so heat lamps give off infrared to warm them.
Which of these is NOT a use of infrared?
Taking pictures of broken bones
Night-vision cameras
TV remote controls
Checking houses for heat leaks
Pictures of broken bones are taken with X-rays, not infrared.
A thermal camera can spot a person in darkness but not behind a thick concrete wall. Why?
Thick concrete blocks the infrared
The person stops giving off heat
Infrared only travels in daylight
Concrete gives off X-rays instead
Infrared passes through air but is absorbed by thick solid walls.
Which objects give off infrared radiation?
All warm objects, including people
Only the Sun and other stars
Only objects that glow bright red
Only devices that use electricity
Every object above absolute zero gives off some infrared, and warmer objects give off more.
How fast does infrared radiation travel through space?
At the speed of light
At the speed of sound
At half the speed of light
At twice the speed of light
Infrared is an electromagnetic wave, so it travels at the speed of light.
sciXsUV: Why is too much UV exposure linked to skin cancer?
It can damage the DNA in skin cells
It can freeze the water in skin cells
It can add extra water to skin cells
It can only affect the hair on skin
UV energy can cause changes in DNA, which may lead cells to grow out of control.
What does a higher SPF number on sunscreen mean?
More protection from sunburn
Less protection from sunburn
A stronger scent
No need to reapply
SPF measures how well sunscreen protects against the UVB rays that cause sunburn.
Why should sunglasses block UV?
UV can damage the eyes
UV makes colours look dull
UV is too bright to look at
UV makes eyes feel warm
Long exposure to UV can harm the cornea and lens of the eye.
Why is snow blindness a risk for skiers?
Snow reflects lots of UV into the eyes
Snow absorbs all of the light
Cold air freezes the eyes
Snow gives off infrared
Fresh snow reflects much of the Sun's UV, which can burn the surface of the eyes.
Why is the UV risk greater on a high mountain?
Thinner air absorbs less UV
Cold air makes UV stronger
Rocks give off their own UV
Mountains reflect radio waves
At high altitude there is less atmosphere above you to absorb the Sun's UV.
When is UV from the Sun usually strongest during the day?
Around midday
Early morning
Late evening
Just after sunset
Around noon the Sun is highest, so its rays pass through the least atmosphere.
Compared with visible light, ultraviolet has a…
shorter wavelength
longer wavelength
lower frequency
slower speed
UV waves are shorter than visible light waves and carry more energy.
Ultraviolet lies just beyond which colour of visible light?
Violet
Red
Orange
Yellow
The name ultraviolet means 'beyond violet', since its wavelengths are just shorter than violet light.
Can humans see ultraviolet light?
No, it is invisible to us
Yes, it looks violet to us
Yes, it looks white to us
Yes, but only on cloudy days
Human eyes cannot detect UV, though some animals can.
Bees can see ultraviolet light. How does this help them?
They see UV patterns on flowers
They see in total darkness
They sense heat from animals
They hear other bees buzzing
Many flowers have UV markings that guide bees to nectar.
Why do banknotes have marks that glow under UV light?
To help detect fake money
To keep the bills cool
To make the bills waterproof
To make the bills heavier
Hidden fluorescent features are hard to copy, so UV lamps help spot counterfeits.
Why do you rarely get sunburned through a closed car side window?
Glass blocks most of the UVB that causes sunburn
Glass blocks all of the visible light
Glass turns the UV into radio waves
Glass reflects all of the sunlight
Ordinary glass absorbs most UVB, though some UVA can still pass through.
Which waves carry more energy than visible light?
Ultraviolet
Infrared
Radio waves
Microwaves
UV has a higher frequency than visible light, so it carries more energy.
Why do curtains and posters near sunny windows fade over time?
UV energy breaks down the dye molecules
UV adds extra water to the dyes
UV cools the dyes until they freeze
UV coats the colours in white paint
UV has enough energy to break the chemical bonds in many dyes.
What is a black light?
A lamp that gives off mostly UV light
A lamp that gives off mostly X-rays
A lamp that gives off no energy
A lamp that absorbs all light
Black lights give off ultraviolet with very little visible light.
Which type of UV is almost completely absorbed by the atmosphere before reaching the ground?
UVC
UVA
UVB
All types equally
UVC is the most energetic type, and the ozone layer and atmosphere absorb nearly all of it.
In Canada, which season usually has the highest UV index?
Summer
Winter
Autumn
Late fall
In summer the Sun is highest in the sky, so UV rays are strongest.
On Canada's scale, how is a UV index of 8 described?
Very high
Low
Moderate
Extreme
A UV index of 8 to 10 is very high, and 11 or more is extreme.
Which is the best way to protect yourself on a high-UV day?
Wear a hat, sunglasses and sunscreen
Stay in the open sun at midday
Skip sunscreen if it is cloudy
Protect only your face and nose
Covering up and using sunscreen reduce the UV reaching your skin and eyes.
Why does being near water or sand increase your UV exposure?
They reflect UV onto your skin
They absorb all UV from above
They turn UV into sound waves
They block UV from the Sun
Water and sand reflect UV, so you get rays from below as well as above.
Why do white shirts glow under a black light?
Brighteners in the fabric absorb UV and give off visible light
The fabric reflects X-rays back into the room
The shirt is much warmer than nearby objects
The fabric makes its own light without any UV
Optical brighteners in detergent are fluorescent, turning invisible UV into visible blue-white light.
Clouding of the eye's lens, called a cataract, can be caused partly by years of…
UV exposure
loud music
eating carrots
reading in dim light
Long-term UV exposure is a known risk factor for cataracts.
sciPER: Lithium is in group 1, the alkali metals, with one valence electron.
Rubidium is in group 1, so it is a very reactive alkali metal.
Cesium sits in group 1, the alkali metals.
Beryllium is in group 2, the alkaline earth metals.
Strontium is in group 2 and has two valence electrons.
Barium is a group 2 element, an alkaline earth metal.
Argon is in group 18, the unreactive noble gases.
Krypton is a group 18 noble gas with a full outer shell.
Xenon is in group 18, the noble gases.
Bromine is in group 17, the halogens, and is a liquid at room temperature.
Iodine is a group 17 element, a halogen.
Zinc is in the central block of the periodic table with the transition metals.
Nickel is in the d-block, among the transition metals.
Silver is a transition metal in group 11.
Gold is a transition metal in group 11, below silver.
Chromium is in the middle block of the table, with the transition metals.
Which group contains elements that are very unreactive gases with full outer shells?
Noble gases already have full valence shells, so they rarely react.
Which group's atoms have one valence electron and react strongly with water?
Group 1 metals easily lose their single valence electron, so they react strongly with water.
Which group's atoms have seven valence electrons?
Halogens in group 17 have seven valence electrons and gain one to form 1− ions.
Atoms in which group usually form ions with a 2+ charge?
Group 2 atoms lose their two valence electrons to form 2+ ions.
What is the group number of the halogens?
The halogens make up group 17, just left of the noble gases.
What is the group number of the noble gases?
The noble gases are in group 18, the far right column.
sciXsBiomol: Which type of biomolecule is described? Cellulose that makes up plant cell walls
Cellulose is a polysaccharide built from glucose units.
Which type of biomolecule is described? Keratin in hair and fingernails
Keratin is a tough structural protein.
Which type of biomolecule is described? Haemoglobin that carries oxygen in red blood cells
Haemoglobin is a protein that binds oxygen.
Which type of biomolecule is described? RNA that carries instructions to the ribosomes
RNA is a nucleic acid made of nucleotides.
Which type of biomolecule is described? Wax that waterproofs the surface of leaves
Waxes are lipids that repel water.
Which type of biomolecule is described? Glycogen stored in the liver and muscles
Glycogen is a polysaccharide animals use to store glucose.
Which type of biomolecule is described? Long chains built from amino acids
Proteins are polymers of amino acids.
Which type of biomolecule is described? Long chains built from nucleotides
Nucleic acids such as DNA and RNA are polymers of nucleotides.
Which type of biomolecule is described? Molecules made of glycerol and fatty acids
Fats and oils are triglycerides made from glycerol and three fatty acids.
Which type of biomolecule is described? Molecules built from simple sugars
Carbohydrates are made from monosaccharides such as glucose.
Which type of biomolecule is described? Cholesterol found in animal cell membranes
Cholesterol is a steroid, a type of lipid.
Which type of biomolecule is described? Actin and myosin that make muscles contract
Actin and myosin are proteins that slide past each other in muscle.
Which type of biomolecule is described? Sucrose, the table sugar in a sugar bowl
Sucrose is a sugar made of glucose and fructose, so it is a carbohydrate.
Which type of biomolecule is described? Chitin in the hard outer skeleton of insects
Which type of biomolecule is described? Blubber that insulates whales and seals
Blubber is mostly fat, which stores energy and insulates.
Which type of biomolecule is described? Genes found on chromosomes
Genes are sections of DNA, a nucleic acid.
Which type of biomolecule is described? Contains the bases A, T, C and G
Adenine, thymine, cytosine and guanine are the bases in DNA.
Which type of biomolecule is described? Collagen that strengthens skin and tendons
Collagen is the most common structural protein in the body.
Which type of biomolecule is described? Lactose, the sugar found in milk
Lactose is a sugar, so it is a carbohydrate.
Which type of biomolecule is described? Insulin, a hormone that lowers blood sugar
Insulin is a small protein made of amino acid chains.
Which element is found in all proteins but not in simple carbohydrates or fats?
Amino acids contain an amino group with nitrogen, while carbohydrates and fats contain only C, H and O.
Which test solution turns blue-black when starch is present?
Iodine reacts with starch to give a blue-black colour.
